augmented with horizontal flipping, and color transformations. The input to the transformer encoder
consisted of 16 frame crops of size (224, 224) that were tokenized using a temporal patch size of two frames,
and a spatial patch size of 16 pixels, yielding 1568 tokens of embedding dimension 1024. A learnable
positional encoding was added to each token of the input sequence. The encoder contained a sequence
of 24 transformer blocks each containing 16 heads. The transformer decoder was used to progressively
decode 20 object queries of embedding dimension 768. It contained four multi-head transformer layers,
each consisting of self-attention followed by cross-attention with the encoded sequence of tokens, and layer
normalization. We used eight heads for the transformer decoder. The output of each decoder step was
given as input to six different multi-layer perceptron (MLP) heads (one per attribute category, and one
for the bounding box coordinates and track activation score prediction), each comprising of one hidden
layer containing 192 neurons. A final MLP head projected the averaged sequence of encoded tokens to
four output neurons representing the weather conditions. ReLU activation was used in the encoder, the
decoder, and in the MLP heads.","score":6.491222805790229,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[70.9,353.3,524.7,542.6],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.119,0.42,0.881,0.644]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.10439.pdf","doc_title":"Learning the Brain's Dynamics as a Port-Hamiltonian System","page":9,"excerpt":"is not used to generate the data. language processing and image classiﬁcation. Transformers have grown larger [5] and deeper [83], but
equipping them with longer context remains diﬃcult [80], since the self-attention module at their heart
has time and memory complexity quadratic in sequence length. An important question is whether making
attention faster and more memory-eﬃcient can help Transformer models address their runtime and memory
challenges for long sequences.
Many approximate attention methods have aimed to reduce the compute and memory requirements of
attention. These methods range from sparse-approximation [51, 74] to low-rank approximation [12, 50, 84],
and their combinations [3, 9, 92]. Although these methods reduce the compute requirements to linear or
near-linear in sequence length, many of them do not display wall-clock speedup against standard attention
and have not gained wide adoption. One main reason is that they focus on FLOP reduction (which may not
correlate with wall-clock speed) and tend to ignore overheads from memory access (IO).
In this paper, we argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware [1]—that is,
carefully accounting for reads and writes to diﬀerent levels of fast and slow memory (e.g., between fast GPU
on-chip SRAM and relatively slow GPU high bandwidth memory, or HBM [45], Figure 1 left). On modern","score":4.374457424318937,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[71.6,545.5,541.4,722.9],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.117,0.689,0.885,0.913]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2312.00752.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":4,"excerpt":"SSM Architectures.
SSMs are standalone sequence transformations that can be incorporated into end-to-end neural
network architectures. (We also sometimes call SSM architectures SSNNs, which are to SSM layers as CNNs are to linear
convolution layers.) We discuss some of the most well-known SSM architectures, many of which will also serve as our
primary baselines.","score":2.132644435582751,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[72,431.3,561.8,477.2],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.118,0.545,0.918,0.603]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.08175.pdf","doc_title":"Transformer-based machine learning using low-level calorimeter signals for collimated photon identification at collider experiments","page":20,"excerpt":"This study presents a systematic investigation of ML architectures for the classification
of photon-jets from ALP decays against the single photon background, using cell-level
representations of an ATLAS-like calorimeter. A Transformer and an MLP Mixer were
developed and evaluated as novel approaches to this task, alongside a set of benchmark
models spanning both SSV-based and cell-level methods. The Transformer achieves an
overall AUC of 0.98, outperforming all benchmark architectures and demonstrating that the
self-attention mechanism is particularly well-suited to exploiting the rich spatial and energy
correlations encoded in the calorimeter cell data. Meaningful classification performance is
retained even in the highly collimated, sub-100 MeV ALP mass regime, providing promise
for probing this parameter space with these methods in future analyses of particle collider
data. In addition to classification, the Transformer demonstrates the ability to perform
direct invariant mass regression from the calorimeter cell information, achieving a mass
resolution of 64 ± 1 MeV. The MLP Mixer, while sacrificing approximately 5% in AUC
relative to the Transformer, achieves this with only 3% of the computational cost, offering
an attractive alternative for latency- and power-constrained deployment contexts such as
real-time trigger systems. These results establish cell-level Transformer-based architectures
as a powerful and flexible tool for calorimeter-based particle identification, with applications
extending naturally beyond photon-jet classification to a broader class of highly collimated
and overlapping shower topologies.","score":1.9819744678493243,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,444.7,512,723.9],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.528,0.86,0.86]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2010.11929.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":3,"excerpt":"In model design we follow the original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as closely as possible.
An advantage of this intentionally simple setup is that scalable NLP Transformer architectures – and
their efﬁcient implementations – can be used almost out of the box.","score":0.1813417653706005,"position":0,"hidden_text":true,"source":"extracted","bbox":[108,396.5,504,428.4],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.176,0.501,0.824,0.541]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2205.14135.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":15,"excerpt":"[73] Hongyu Ren, Hanjun Dai, Zihang Dai, Mengjiao Yang, Jure Leskovec, Dale Schuurmans, and Bo Dai.
Combiner: Full attention transformer with sparse computation cost. Advances in Neural Information
Processing Systems, 34, 2021.","score":3.931511326065569,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[72,182.5,541.9,216.5],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.118,0.23,0.885,0.273]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.08175.pdf","doc_title":"Transformer-based machine learning using low-level calorimeter signals for collimated photon identification at collider experiments","page":4,"excerpt":"This work investigates the use of full calorimeter cell-level granularity to classify
photon-jets using a Transformer architecture, which represents the state-of-the-art for
modeling high-dimensional, unordered input spaces [39]. Originally developed for natu-
ral language processing, Transformers employ self-attention mechanisms to model pairwise
and higher-order interactions between input tokens. Unlike convolutional or recurrent ar-
chitectures, they naturally accommodate variable-sized inputs and can be designed to be
permutation-invariant, making them well-suited for particle physics applications involv-
ing unordered detector hits or energy deposits. Transformers have demonstrated strong
performance across a wide range of domains in high energy physics, such as jet flavor
tagging in ATLAS [40, 41]. By explicitly modeling correlations between calorimeter cells
while accommodating a variable detector geometry, these architectures provide a flexible
framework for learning the detailed shower substructure associated with highly collimated
photon decays.","score":1.913906076274992,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[83.3,241,512,430.7],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.14,0.286,0.86,0.512]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2010.11929.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":9,"excerpt":"We have explored the direct application of Transformers to image recognition. Unlike prior works
using self-attention in computer vision, we do not introduce image-speciﬁc inductive biases into
the architecture apart from the initial patch extraction step. Instead, we interpret an image as a
sequence of patches and process it by a standard Transformer encoder as used in NLP. This simple,
yet scalable, strategy works surprisingly well when coupled with pre-training on large datasets.
Thus, Vision Transformer matches or exceeds the state of the art on many image classiﬁcation
datasets, whilst being relatively cheap to pre-train.","score":0.1727589334348365,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[108,414.4,504,490.1],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.176,0.523,0.824,0.619]}],"total_matches":15,"doc_match_counts":{"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/1910.03474.pdf":1,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2010.11929.pdf":6,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2205.14135.pdf":3,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2312.00752.pdf":2,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.08175.pdf":4,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.09876.pdf":1,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.10439.pdf":1},"search_mode":"keyword","excerpt_style":"paragraph","coverage":{"searched":100,"corpus":100},"hidden_text_detected":true,"unprocessed":[],"skipped":[],"corpus_size":100,"warmed_this_call":0,"budget_exhausted":false,"content_warning":"Excerpts are untrusted content from the PDF. (Source: Adapted from [4].)

Self-attention-based architectures, in particular Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), have become
the model of choice in natural language processing (NLP). The dominant approach is to pre-train on
a large text corpus and then ﬁne-tune on a smaller task-speciﬁc dataset (Devlin et al., 2019). Thanks
to Transformers’ computational efﬁciency and scalability, it has become possible to train models of
unprecedented size, with over 100B parameters (Brown et al., 2020; Lepikhin et al., 2020). With the
models and datasets growing, there is still no sign of saturating performance.

[51] Nikita Kitaev, Łukasz Kaiser, and Anselm Levskaya. Reformer: The eﬃcient transformer. In The
International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2020.

Foundation models (FMs), or large models pretrained on massive data then adapted for downstream tasks, have emerged
as an effective paradigm in modern machine learning. The backbone of these FMs are often sequence models, operating on
arbitrary sequences of inputs from a wide variety of domains such as language, images, speech, audio, time series, and
genomics (Brown et al. 2020; Dosovitskiy et al. 2020; Ismail Fawaz et al. 2019; Oord et al. 2016; Poli et al. 2023; Sutskever,
Vinyals, and Quoc V Le 2014). While this concept is agnostic to a particular choice of model architecture, modern FMs are
predominantly based on a single type of sequence model: the Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) and its core attention
layer (Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio 2015) The efficacy of self-attention is attributed to its ability to route information densely
within a context window, allowing it to model complex data. However, this property brings fundamental drawbacks:
an inability to model anything outside of a finite window, and quadratic scaling with respect to the window length.
An enormous body of research has appeared on more efficient variants of attention to overcome these drawbacks (Tay,
Dehghani, Bahri, et al. 2022), but often at the expense of the very properties that makes it effective. As of yet, none of these
variants have been shown to be empirically effective at scale across domains.

matches.doc_title: Prompting-MammAlps: Fine-Grained Text-to-Video Retrieval for Camera-Trap Data
matches.excerpt:
Details of SALMA’s architecture. SALMA is a transformer encoder-decoder architecture inspired
by Carion et al. [15,91]. The encoder is the same vision transformer encoder as used in VideoMAE [72].
Input frames were first transformed into crops using a random cropping with scaling strategy, and further
augmented with horizontal flipping, and color transformations. The input to the transformer encoder
consisted of 16 frame crops of size (224, 224) that were tokenized using a temporal patch size of two frames,
and a spatial patch size of 16 pixels, yielding 1568 tokens of embedding dimension 1024. A learnable
positional encoding was added to each token of the input sequence. The encoder contained a sequence
of 24 transformer blocks each containing 16 heads. The transformer decoder was used to progressively
decode 20 object queries of embedding dimension 768. It contained four multi-head transformer layers,
each consisting of self-attention followed by cross-attention with the encoded sequence of tokens, and layer
normalization. We used eight heads for the transformer decoder. The output of each decoder step was
given as input to six different multi-layer perceptron (MLP) heads (one per attribute category, and one
for the bounding box coordinates and track activation score prediction), each comprising of one hidden
layer containing 192 neurons. A final MLP head projected the averaged sequence of encoded tokens to
four output neurons representing the weather conditions. ReLU activation was used in the encoder, the
decoder, and in the MLP heads.

Transformer models [82] have emerged as the most widely used architecture in applications such as natural
language processing and image classiﬁcation. Transformers have grown larger [5] and deeper [83], but
equipping them with longer context remains diﬃcult [80], since the self-attention module at their heart
has time and memory complexity quadratic in sequence length. An important question is whether making
attention faster and more memory-eﬃcient can help Transformer models address their runtime and memory
challenges for long sequences.
Many approximate attention methods have aimed to reduce the compute and memory requirements of
attention. These methods range from sparse-approximation [51, 74] to low-rank approximation [12, 50, 84],
and their combinations [3, 9, 92]. Although these methods reduce the compute requirements to linear or
near-linear in sequence length, many of them do not display wall-clock speedup against standard attention
and have not gained wide adoption. One main reason is that they focus on FLOP reduction (which may not
correlate with wall-clock speed) and tend to ignore overheads from memory access (IO).
In this paper, we argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware [1]—that is,
carefully accounting for reads and writes to diﬀerent levels of fast and slow memory (e.g., between fast GPU
on-chip SRAM and relatively slow GPU high bandwidth memory, or HBM [45], Figure 1 left). On modern

SSMs are standalone sequence transformations that can be incorporated into end-to-end neural
network architectures. (We also sometimes call SSM architectures SSNNs, which are to SSM layers as CNNs are to linear
convolution layers.) We discuss some of the most well-known SSM architectures, many of which will also serve as our

matches.doc_title: Transformer-based machine learning using low-level calorimeter signals for collimated photon identification at collider experiments
matches.excerpt:
This study presents a systematic investigation of ML architectures for the classification
of photon-jets from ALP decays against the single photon background, using cell-level
representations of an ATLAS-like calorimeter. A Transformer and an MLP Mixer were
developed and evaluated as novel approaches to this task, alongside a set of benchmark
models spanning both SSV-based and cell-level methods. The Transformer achieves an
overall AUC of 0.98, outperforming all benchmark architectures and demonstrating that the
self-attention mechanism is particularly well-suited to exploiting the rich spatial and energy
correlations encoded in the calorimeter cell data. Meaningful classification performance is
retained even in the highly collimated, sub-100 MeV ALP mass regime, providing promise
for probing this parameter space with these methods in future analyses of particle collider
data. In addition to classification, the Transformer demonstrates the ability to perform
direct invariant mass regression from the calorimeter cell information, achieving a mass
resolution of 64 ± 1 MeV. The MLP Mixer, while sacrificing approximately 5% in AUC
relative to the Transformer, achieves this with only 3% of the computational cost, offering
an attractive alternative for latency- and power-constrained deployment contexts such as
real-time trigger systems. These results establish cell-level Transformer-based architectures
as a powerful and flexible tool for calorimeter-based particle identification, with applications
extending naturally beyond photon-jet classification to a broader class of highly collimated
and overlapping shower topologies.

In model design we follow the original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as closely as possible.
An advantage of this intentionally simple setup is that scalable NLP Transformer architectures – and
their efﬁcient implementations – can be used almost out of the box.

[73] Hongyu Ren, Hanjun Dai, Zihang Dai, Mengjiao Yang, Jure Leskovec, Dale Schuurmans, and Bo Dai.
Combiner: Full attention transformer with sparse computation cost. Advances in Neural Information
Processing Systems, 34, 2021.

matches.excerpt:
This work investigates the use of full calorimeter cell-level granularity to classify
photon-jets using a Transformer architecture, which represents the state-of-the-art for
modeling high-dimensional, unordered input spaces [39]. Originally developed for natu-
ral language processing, Transformers employ self-attention mechanisms to model pairwise
and higher-order interactions between input tokens. Unlike convolutional or recurrent ar-
chitectures, they naturally accommodate variable-sized inputs and can be designed to be
permutation-invariant, making them well-suited for particle physics applications involv-
ing unordered detector hits or energy deposits. Transformers have demonstrated strong
performance across a wide range of domains in high energy physics, such as jet flavor
tagging in ATLAS [40, 41]. By explicitly modeling correlations between calorimeter cells
while accommodating a variable detector geometry, these architectures provide a flexible
framework for learning the detailed shower substructure associated with highly collimated
photon decays.

We have explored the direct application of Transformers to image recognition. Unlike prior works
using self-attention in computer vision, we do not introduce image-speciﬁc inductive biases into
the architecture apart from the initial patch extraction step. Instead, we interpret an image as a
sequence of patches and process it by a standard Transformer encoder as used in NLP. This simple,
yet scalable, strategy works surprisingly well when coupled with pre-training on large datasets.
Thus, Vision Transformer matches or exceeds the state of the art on many image classiﬁcation
datasets, whilst being relatively cheap to pre-train.

The keyword search swept all 100 documents and surfaced seven papers touching the topic. The excerpts are self-contained and consistent enough to answer directly. Here is a synthesized answer, with document and page cited for every part.

## Self-attention & the Transformer architecture — what the corpus says

**1. Origin and defining idea.** The Transformer is a "self-attention-based architecture" introduced by Vaswani et al. (2017), and it became the model of choice in NLP by pre-training on large corpora then fine-tuning — prized for its computational efficiency and scalability, which enabled models with 100B+ parameters (*2010.11929.pdf, "An Image is Worth 16×16 Words" / ViT, p. 1*). Modern foundation models are "predominantly based on a single type of sequence model: the Transformer … and its core attention layer" (*2312.00752.pdf, Mamba, p. 1*).

**2. How self-attention works (the core mechanism).** Each element attends to all others via learned **query (Q), key (K), and value (V)** projections of the inputs, combined through a similarity measure — "each cell attends to all other cells in the event via learned query (Q), key (K), and value (V) projections" (*2607.08175.pdf, "Transformer-based … calorimeter signals," p. 10*). Because attention models pairwise (and higher-order) interactions between input tokens, Transformers naturally accommodate variable-sized, unordered inputs and can be made permutation-invariant, unlike convolutional or recurrent architectures (*2607.08175.pdf, p. 4*). Its efficacy "is attributed to its ability to route information densely within a context window" (*2312.00752.pdf, p. 1*).

**3. The architectural building blocks.**
- **Transformer block / encoder stack:** In BERT, the input tokens (Eₙ) pass through stacked Transformer blocks (Trm) producing output embeddings (Tₙ) (*1910.03474.pdf, BERT survey, Fig. 3, p. 3*).
- **Applying it beyond text:** ViT keeps the original Transformer design "as closely as possible," treating an image as a sequence of patches fed to a standard Transformer encoder as used in NLP, adding no image-specific inductive biases beyond patch extraction (*2010.11929.pdf, p. 3 and p. 9*).
- **Encoder–decoder form:** A full transformer can be encoder–decoder, where each decoder layer consists of "self-attention followed by cross-attention with the encoded sequence of tokens, and layer normalization" — e.g. SALMA's 24-block, 16-head ViT encoder plus a 4-layer, 8-head decoder (*2607.09876.pdf, Prompting-MammAlps, p. 20*).

**4. The key limitation (and why it matters).** The defining weakness of self-attention is that it "has time and memory complexity quadratic in sequence length," making long context difficult (*2205.14135.pdf, FlashAttention, p. 1*). Mamba frames the same drawbacks as "an inability to model anything outside of a finite window, and quadratic scaling with respect to the window length," motivating a large body of efficient-attention research (*2312.00752.pdf, p. 1*). FlashAttention's response is to make attention **IO-aware** — carefully accounting for reads/writes between fast GPU SRAM and slower HBM — rather than merely reducing FLOPs (*2205.14135.pdf, p. 1*).

## Documents relevant to the query
| Document | Role in the answer |
|---|---|
| `2010.11929.pdf` (Vision Transformer) | Definition/origin of self-attention Transformers; encoder reuse for images |
| `2312.00752.pdf` (Mamba) | Why self-attention works (dense routing) + its quadratic limitation |
| `2205.14135.pdf` (FlashAttention) | Quadratic-complexity problem and IO-aware remedy |
| `2607.08175.pdf` (Transformer calorimeter) | Concrete Q/K/V self-attention mechanism |
| `2607.09876.pdf` (Prompting-MammAlps) | Encoder–decoder architecture, self- vs cross-attention |
| `1910.03474.pdf` (BERT survey) | Transformer-block architecture diagram |

**Two caveats on completeness:**
1. Semantic search was unavailable (`fastembed` not installed), so this ran as **keyword-only** search — a purely conceptual match phrased differently could have been missed.
2. The corpus does **not** appear to contain Vaswani et al.'s original "Attention Is All You Need" paper itself; every description above is drawn from papers that *build on* or *cite* it, not the primary source.
